title: Weather Alert: Typhoon Champi Shuts Schools and Offices Across Taiwan
summaryZh: ⚠️ 颱風羌彼來襲，全台除金門外停班停課，北部山區恐降900毫米雨。
summaryHi: ⚠️ तूफ़ान चाम्पी: किनमेन छोड़ पूरे ताइवान में स्कूल-दफ़्तर बंद, भारी बारिश की चेतावनी।
summaryEs: ⚠️ Tifón Champi: cierran escuelas y oficinas en casi todo Taiwán; lluvias torrenciales.

summaryKo: ⚠️ 태풍 참피 접근, 진먼 제외 대만 전역 휴교·휴무…폭우 경계.
summaryEn: ⚠️ Typhoon Champi closes schools and offices across Taiwan; heavy rain and strong winds until Saturday.
paragraphs: Typhoon Champi is lashing Taiwan with powerful winds and torrential rain, prompting the Central Weather Administration (CWA) to keep sea and land warnings in force. Schools and offices were closed on Friday, October 23, in every city and county except Kinmen.

As of Friday morning, the storm was about 300 kilometres south-east of the island, with maximum sustained winds of 155km/h and gusts reaching 191km/h. Forecasters expect it to slow down and pass within about 80 kilometres of Taiwan late on Friday night or early on Saturday, and landfall cannot be ruled out. Gale-force winds are expected across the whole island.

The heaviest rain is forecast until Saturday morning, with mountainous parts of northern and north-eastern Taiwan possibly receiving 600 to 900 millimetres. The mountains of Yilan face extremely torrential rain, raising the risk of landslides and debris flows. More than 1,200 people have been evacuated, mostly in Hualien and Yilan.

Transport has been severely disrupted. Almost 1,000 flights were cancelled between Thursday and Friday morning, nine ferry routes were suspended, and all express services on the main rail lines were halted, although the high-speed rail ran as usual. Alishan and many national parks and trails are closed.
The typhoon is expected to move away on Saturday afternoon. Officials urge the public to avoid rivers, beaches and mountains throughout the long weekend, even once the storm has passed.
Typhoon Champi is very close to Taiwan now. The weather office has warnings for the land and the sea. On Friday, schools and offices are closed in almost all of Taiwan. Only Kinmen is open as normal.

The storm will be closest to Taiwan from Friday night to Saturday morning. It may come onto land. There will be very strong wind on the whole island. In the mountains in the north and north-east, there may be 600 to 900 millimetres of rain.

Many trips have stopped. Hundreds of flights are cancelled. Many boats to small islands are not running. Fast trains on the normal railway are cancelled, but the high-speed train is running. Alishan and many mountain parks are closed.
The storm will go away on Saturday afternoon or evening. The government says: do not go to the beach, rivers or mountains, even after the storm. Stay safe at home.

Typhoon Champi is bringing strong winds and very heavy rain to Taiwan. The Central Weather Administration (CWA) has issued sea and land warnings, and on Friday, October 23, schools and offices were closed in almost every city and county. Only Kinmen worked as normal.

On Friday morning the typhoon was about 300 kilometres south-east of Taiwan, with winds of around 155 kilometres per hour. It is moving slowly and is expected to come closest late on Friday night and early on Saturday. It could even reach land. The heaviest rain will fall until Saturday morning, and mountains in the north and north-east may get 600 to 900 millimetres.

Travel is badly affected. About 977 flights were cancelled from Thursday to Friday morning, and 96 ferry trips were stopped. All express trains on the main railway lines were cancelled on Friday, but the high-speed rail ran normally. Alishan and other mountain areas are closed.

The storm should move away on Saturday afternoon, and the warnings may end then. The government asks people to stay away from rivers, beaches and mountains during the long weekend, even after the storm leaves. Do not go to the coast to watch the waves.

Taiwan is bracing for the worst of Typhoon Champi, a slow-moving storm that has already brought much of the island to a standstill. With sea and land warnings in force, every city and county except Kinmen suspended classes and office work on Friday, October 23.

Although the typhoon has weakened slightly, it remained formidable on Friday morning, packing sustained winds of 155km/h and gusts of up to 191km/h some 300 kilometres off the south-east coast. The Central Weather Administration (CWA) expects it to pass within roughly 80 kilometres of Taiwan from late Friday night into Saturday morning, and it has not ruled out a direct landfall.

Rainfall is the gravest concern. Mountainous areas in the north and north-east could be drenched with 600 to 900 millimetres by Saturday, and extremely torrential rain advisories cover the mountains of Yilan. Authorities have evacuated more than 1,200 residents, including people living below a landslide-formed lake on the Wanli River in Hualien.

The disruption to travel is extensive: nearly 1,000 flights have been scrapped, nine ferry routes suspended and express trains on the main railway lines cancelled, though the high-speed rail has kept running. Alishan, Yushan National Park and numerous trails are off limits.

Champi is forecast to drift away on Saturday afternoon, when warnings may be lifted. With a long weekend under way, the premier has urged people to keep clear of rivers, beaches and mountains even after the storm has gone.

Typhoon Champi has caused widespread disruption across Taiwan, compelling the authorities to close schools and offices in every city and county except Kinmen on Friday, October 23. The Central Weather Administration (CWA) has maintained both sea and land warnings as the storm advances slowly towards the island.

On Friday morning, the typhoon was located approximately 300 kilometres south-east of Taiwan, with sustained winds of 155km/h. Forecasters anticipate that it will come within roughly 80 kilometres of the coast between late Friday night and early Saturday, and a landfall remains possible. Consequently, gale-force winds are expected to affect the entire island.

Of particular concern is the prospect of intense rainfall. Mountainous regions in the north and north-east may receive between 600 and 900 millimetres by Saturday, significantly increasing the likelihood of landslides and flooding. As a precaution, over 1,200 residents, predominantly in Hualien and Yilan, have been evacuated.

The storm has also severely affected transport. Nearly 1,000 flights have been cancelled, nine ferry routes have been suspended, and express rail services have been withdrawn, although the high-speed rail continues to operate normally. In addition, popular destinations such as Alishan have been closed.
The typhoon is projected to move away on Saturday afternoon. Nevertheless, the government has strongly advised the public to avoid rivers, beaches and mountainous areas throughout the long weekend.
